Launceston
LAWN-stun
n. (the Cornish castle and gaol town where George Fox was imprisoned in 1656 in the pit called Doomsdale)
Cornish Lann Stefan, the church enclosure of Stephen, from lann, a church site; the Old English castle name was Dunheved.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Launceston is the Cornish town on the Tamar below the Norman castle of Dunheved, long the county gaol and the seat of the Cornish assizes. Its place in the dictionary is one imprisonment. In 1656 George Fox, with Edward Pyot and William Salt, was taken on the road near St Ives and brought before the justices at Launceston; he refused to remove his hat in court, was fined for contempt and committed, and the three were put into the underground cell called Doomsdale, which Fox describes in his journal as filthy beyond description and never cleaned, where the gaoler charged them for everything and poured the ordure of the prison in upon them. They were held nine weeks until Major-General Desborough had them released. Fox was neither Reformed nor confessional, and the dictionary holds his doctrine of the inner light to be a grave error that puts an immediate illumination in the place of the written Word. It records the gaol all the same, because the treatment of a man for refusing a hat is not answered by the errors in his theology, and because a Protestant magistracy that filled its prisons over such matters was storing up the arguments that would be used against itself.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a gaol as a prison; contempt of court as disobedience to its authority; a dungeon as a dark subterraneous prison; forbearance as the exercise of patience; and testimony as witness borne.

expand to see more

GAOL, n. A prison; a place for the confinement of debtors and criminals.

CONTEMPT, n. In law, disobedience to the rules and orders of a court, which is a punishable offence.

DUNGEON, n. A close prison; or a deep dark place of confinement; originally the tower or keep of a castle.

FORBEARANCE, n. The exercise of patience; long suffering; indulgence toward those who injure us.

TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing a fact; witness.

Key Scripture

Act 7:60 — "And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he fell asleep."

2Ti 3:12 — "Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution."

Joh 16:2 — "They shall put you out of the synagogues: yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service."

Heb 12:4 — "Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin."

Modern Corruption

Cornish gaol town where George Fox and two companions were held nine weeks in 1656 in the underground cell called Doomsdale, committed for refusing to uncover in court.

expand to see more

The corruption named here is ours, and it is the use of the gaol for matters of conscience and ceremony. Fox was committed over a hat; the fine was for contempt and the contempt was his refusal of a gesture he judged to be flattery of men. Whatever is to be said against his theology, and the dictionary says a good deal against it, nothing in it warranted Doomsdale. Our Lord warned His disciples that the men who handled them worst would do it as a service to God, for the time comes “that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2), and that is precisely the temper of a magistracy that gaols men for gestures. Stephen's dying word is the standing pattern for the sufferer, “Lord, lay not this sin to their charge” (Act 7:60).

The second paragraph marks the limits of the sympathy, because the dictionary will not purchase a point against persecution at the price of the doctrine. Fox taught an inner light sufficient for salvation and set it above the Scriptures; the Reformed answer is that the Spirit speaks in and by the Word and never apart from it, and the Quaker scheme, for all its courage under the lash, cut the ground from under preaching and ordinance alike. Both things stand together. Paul tells Timothy that persecution is the ordinary portion of godliness, “all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12), and the writer to the Hebrews reminds a complaining church of the measure actually taken from it, “Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin” (Heb 12:4). An English dissenter reading of Doomsdale in the sixteen-eighties would have found it a nearer prophecy than he liked.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dioko (G1377), to persecute; Greek latreia-related latreuo, to render service; Greek koimao (G2837), to fall asleep in death.

expand to see more

Greek koimao (G2837) — to put to sleep, of death to fall asleep; “when he had said this, he fell asleep”, Acts 7:60.

Greek hamartia (G266) — sin, a missing of the mark; “lay not this sin to their charge”, Acts 7:60.

Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, to persecute; “shall suffer persecution”, 2 Timothy 3:12.

Greek aposunagogos (G656) — expelled from the synagogue; “They shall put you out of the synagogues”, John 16:2.

Greek antagonizomai (G464) — to struggle against; “striving against sin”, Hebrews 12:4.

Usage

"“Lord, lay not this sin to their charge” (Act 7:60) — nine weeks in Doomsdale, 1656."

"“whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2) — a committal over an uncovered head."

"“Ye have not yet resisted unto blood” (Heb 12:4) — the measure English dissent would soon be given."
